stem: Four boys and three girls are to be seated in a row. In how many ways can they be seated so that all three girls sit together?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Treat the 3 girls as one block: 4 boys + 1 block = 5 units. These 5 units can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. The 3 girls within their block can be internally arranged in 3! = 6 ways. Total = 5! x 3! = 120 x 6 = 720.
Computed 7! = 5040, the total unrestricted arrangements without applying the girls-together constraint.
Computed 4! x 3! = 24 x 6 = 144, forming only 4 units instead of 5 (treated the block as replacing one boy rather than adding one extra unit to 4 boys).
Computed C(7,3) = 35 for choosing positions then multiplied by 6 = 210, confusing selection of positions with the block-arrangement method.

explanation: Bundle the 3 girls into one block. Now 5 units (4 boys + 1 block) can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. The girls rearrange internally in 3! = 6 ways. Product: 120 x 6 = 720.

explanation_sections.punchline: Gluing the girls into one block converts a 7-seat problem into a 5-unit problem, then multiply by internal arrangements: 5! x 3! = 720.
explanation_sections.approach: Classify as an arrangement with a group-together constraint. Step 1 - merge the constrained group into a single block, counting the block as one unit. Step 2 - count external arrangements of the resulting (n - group_size + 1) units: here 4 + 1 = 5 units -> 5!. Step 3 - count internal arrangements of the group: 3!. Step 4 - multiply: 5! x 3! = 120 x 6 = 720.
explanation_sections.lesson: When a subset must stay together, replace it with a single block. The new unit count is (total - group_size + 1), and you multiply by (group_size)! for internal arrangements.
explanation_sections.timing: 70-80 s. Trap: computing 4! x 3! = 144 by treating the 4 boys as the only external units and forgetting the block itself is a 5th unit.
